q: What is the minimum slab thickness in mm of a house slab at the ground floor?
n: A ground-floor slab on grade for a house is typically at least 100 mm thick. Source: ACI 332 (Residential Code Requirements for Structural Concrete); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (concrete slabs on grade).

q: A reinforced concrete beam is stripped from its formwork and numerous honeycombs are observed along the sides and bottom face. Assuming the mix proportions were correct and formwork leakage was minimal, which construction deficiency is the MOST likely cause of the honeycombing?
o: Excessive water in the mix causing increased workability and delayed setting
Excessive concrete cover that reduced bond between the reinforcement and surrounding concrete
Prolonged curing that allowed excessive hydration of the cement paste
Inadequate vibration and consolidation, preventing the concrete from fully filling voids and surrounding the reinforcement
n: With a correct mix and tight forms, honeycombing usually comes from poor vibration and consolidation, which leaves voids around the bars. Source: ACI 309R (Guide for Consolidation of Concrete); PCA, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

q: In general, construction joints are located ___ of the spans of slabs.
n: Construction joints in floors are located within the middle third of slab, beam and girder spans, where shear is low. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 426.5.6 (ACI 318-14, 26.5.6.2).

q: A wall used to hold back the surrounding soil to keep it from entering the basement or crawl space. It also helps to keep moisture from entering.
n: A foundation wall encloses a basement or crawl space. It holds back the surrounding soil and helps keep out moisture. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (Foundation Walls).

q: A wall designed and constructed to resist the lateral pressure of the soil when the desired ground elevation exceeds the angle of repose of the soil.
n: A retaining wall resists lateral soil pressure where the grade change is steeper than the soil's angle of repose. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8 (Retaining Walls).

q: A huge retaining wall which relies on its weight to resist horizontal soil pressure and achieve stability.
n: A gravity wall relies on its own mass for stability against horizontal soil pressure. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8.

q: This retaining wall uses tie-backs which are driven deep into the ground behind the wall thereby allowing it to resist pressure from the retained soil.
n: An anchored wall uses tiebacks driven deep into the soil behind it to resist the retained earth. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 9 (Anchored Sheet Pile Walls).

q: This retaining wall works on the principle of leverage. It has a thinner stem and uses the weight of the backfill soil to resist sliding and overturning.
n: A cantilever wall has a thin stem on a base slab. The weight of backfill on the heel resists sliding and overturning. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8.

q: This retaining wall has buttresses attached on its inside face to further resist lateral forces.
n: A counterfort wall has buttress-like counterforts tied to its inside (backfill) face. These help the stem and base resist lateral forces. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8.

q: To prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup behind a retaining wall, which feature is typically integrated into the wall design to allow trapped water to escape, often spaced at regular intervals and lined with filter fabric or gravel?
n: Weep holes, backed by gravel or filter fabric, drain water from the backfill so hydrostatic pressure does not build up. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8 (Drainage of Retaining Walls).

q: Which of the following structural elements is typically constructed using wire mesh cages filled with rocks or rubble, and is commonly used for slope stabilization, erosion control, and retaining walls?
n: Gabions are wire-mesh cages filled with rock, used for slope stabilization, erosion control and retaining walls. Source: ASTM A975 (Gabions); DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 511.

q: During a geohazard assessment along Kennon Road, engineers observed several retaining walls showing signs of outward movement after continuous rainfall. The saturated backfill increased lateral earth pressure, raising the risk of sliding along the base. According to standard retaining wall stability requirements, retaining walls must be designed so that the resisting forces (primarily base friction and passive resistance, if considered) are at least how many times greater than the lateral earth forces acting on the wall?
n: Retaining walls need a factor of safety of at least 1.5 against sliding: resisting forces must be at least 1.5 times the driving lateral force. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 307 (retaining walls); Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Ch. 8.

q: Which material is commonly used in civil engineering to improve soil stability, provide drainage, and prevent erosion by acting as a permeable barrier between different soil layers—typically anchored by trenching, pinning, or overlaying with aggregate fill?
n: Geotextiles are permeable fabrics that separate, filter and drain between soil layers and control erosion. They are anchored by trenching, pinning or aggregate cover. Source: ASTM D4439; DPWH Item 1600 series (geotextiles).

q: Which is used to resist lateral forces?
n: Shear walls are vertical elements designed specifically to resist lateral (wind and seismic) forces. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 208 (Seismic-force-resisting systems: bearing wall and building frame systems).

q: Where is the shear wall located?
n: Shear walls are commonly placed around elevator shafts and stairwells, forming a stiff core. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (Lateral Stability); Taranath, Structural Analysis and Design of Tall Buildings.

q: What is positive shear in beams?
o: When analyzing a beam section, it causes a-counter-clockwise rotation of the section
On the right side of the beam, the shear force acts upward.
On the left side of the beam, the shear force acts upward.
On the left side of the beam, the shear force acts downward.
n: By the usual sign convention, shear is positive when the resultant on the left of the section acts upward (and on the right, downward). This tends to rotate the segment clockwise. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6 (sign convention).

q: Which is true about positive bending in beams?
o: The greatest stress can be found at the transition between the compressive and tensile regions, which is at the neutral axis.
n: Positive (sagging) bending stretches the bottom fibers and compresses the top fibers, giving a concave-upward curve. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: A simply supported reinforced concrete beam is subjected to a uniformly distributed load. At midspan, where:the positive bending moment is greatest, what condition exists at the extreme top fibers of the beam?
o: Torsion, because the beam rotates about its longitudinal axis under gravity loading.
Compression, because sagging flexure shortens the upper fibers while elongating the lower fibers.
Shear, because the maximum internal force at midspan is transferred through the neutral axis.
Tension, because the self-weight of the beam pulls the upper fibers apart near midspan.
n: Under sagging moment at midspan, the top fibers shorten (compression) and the bottom fibers lengthen (tension). Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 6.

q: A load bearing str uctural clement with a flange at the top but none at the bottom.
n: A T-beam has a flange at the top (the slab acting with the beam) and no flange at the bottom. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 406.3.2 (T-beam construction).

q: It is fabricated by filling a steel shell with concrete.
n: A Lally column is a steel tube (shell) filled with concrete. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (Columns).

q: Trademarked large, reinforced cardboard tubes used in creating columns wherein concrete is poured into the cardboard.
n: Sonotube is the trademarked reinforced cardboard tube used as a disposable form for round concrete columns. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (formwork).

q: When a heavy object such as a cabinet, condenser unit, or shelving system is hung on a wall, the load does not act through the wall's centroid but instead applies a force at some distance from it, creating a bending moment on the wall. What type of load is this?
n: A load acting away from a member's centroid is eccentric. It creates a bending moment in addition to the direct force. Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, Ch. 8 (Combined Loadings).

q: It refers to the inherent weight of the building components including the structure's own mass.
n: The inherent weight of building components, including the structure's own mass, is the intrinsic (dead) load. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 204 (Dead Loads).

q: It refers to the self-weight of the various building components
n: Dead load is the self-weight of building components and permanent fixed equipment. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 204.

q: It refers to sudden forces resulting from dynamic events, e.g., machinery operation.
n: Impact loads are sudden dynamic forces, such as those from machinery or moving equipment. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 205.8 (Impact Loads).

q: It refers to temporary loads due to occupancy such as furniture, equipment and people.
n: Live loads come from use and occupancy: people, furniture, movable equipment. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 205.

q: Live loads are often described as
n: Live loads are movable and variable in magnitude and position. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 205.

q: The Seismic Importance Factor is a multiplier used in structural design to account for the criticality of a building during an earthquake. What is the seismic importance factor of essential facilities
n: Essential facilities (Occupancy Category I) have a seismic importance factor I = 1.50. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 208-1.

q: During an earthquake, a structure's ability to withstand seismic forces relies on how well its materials dissipate, deform controllable, and resist sudden failure. Which material characteristic of steel is the most detrimental to an earthquake resistance due to its tendency to cause abrupt structural collapse when subjected to intense ground motion?
n: High hardness in steel goes with brittleness. Hard, brittle steel cannot deform and dissipate energy, so it fails abruptly under strong shaking. Ductility is the desirable property. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 208 (ductile detailing); Salmon & Johnson, Steel Structures, Ch. 2.

q: In the seismic design of steel moment-resisting frames, which type of connection is typically used to ensure full moment transfer between beam and column flanges, accommodate plastic hinge formation away from the column face, and comply with AISC and NSCP 2015 requirements for ductility and energy dissipation?
n: Welded beam-flange-to-column connections (e.g., WUF-W, RBS) give full moment transfer and meet the seismic ductility requirements for special moment frames. Source: AISC 358 (Prequalified Connections); NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 522.

q: During the seismic detailing review of a steel frame, the engineer must determine which beam-to-column joint can function as a moment-resisting connection, meaning it can transfer bending moment, restrain rotation, and contribute to the building's lateral stiffness. Which of the following qualifies as a true moment-resisting connection?
n: Welding both flanges and the web develops the beam's moment, restrains rotation and adds lateral stiffness. Shear tabs and clip angles are simple (shear) connections. Source: AISC 360-16, Sec. B3.4 (Fully Restrained Moment Connections).

q: In structural steel framing, why are moment-resisting connections often preferred when architectural flexibility and unobstructed interior spaces are required?
o: They eliminate the need for columns by transferring all loads directly to the foundation.
They increase the dead load of the structure, improving resistance to overturning.
They provide lateral stability through the transfer of bending moments, reducing the need for diagonal bracing that may interfere with space planning.
They resist only axial forces, making them more efficient than conventional shear connections.
n: Moment connections give lateral stability through frame action. No diagonal braces are needed to obstruct the plan. Source: AISC 360-16, Sec. B3.4; Taranath, Structural Analysis and Design of Tall Buildings.

q: Which seismic technology is used in the Tokyo Skytree to reduce structural sway and absorb earthquake energy?
n: The Tokyo Skytree's central reinforced-concrete shaft (shinbashira) is separated from the steel frame and acts as a counterweight, like a tuned mass damper, cutting sway by up to about half. Source: Nikken Sekkei, Tokyo Skytree structural design (2012).

q: What is the primary purpose of lateral bracing in structural systems?
o: To support vertical loads from slabs and beams
To reduce the weight of structural steel components
To increase the compressive strength of concrete members
To prevent buckling and resist horizontal forces
n: Lateral bracing prevents members from buckling and gives the structure resistance to horizontal forces. Source: AISC 360-16, Appendix 6 (Member Stability Bracing).

q: Which fastening method is most commonly used in modern bridge construction due to its ease of installation, inspection, and maintenance?
n: High-strength bolts are the most common field connection in modern bridges. They are easy to install, inspect and maintain compared with field welding or rivets. Source: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, Sec. 6.13.2.

q: As per NBCP, what is the minimum design live load of the first floor of Group A dwellings, ensuring structural safety and compliance with engineering standards?
n: In Group A dwellings, the first-floor live load must be at least 200 kg/m². Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Live Loads.

q: As per NBCP, what is the minimum design live load of the second floor of Group A dwellings, ensuring structural safety and compliance with engineering standards?
n: The second-floor live load for Group A dwellings must be at least 150 kg/m². Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Live Loads.

q: As per NBCP, what is the minimum design wind load for roofs of Group A dwellings, considering vertical projection?
n: The roof wind load for Group A dwellings must be at least 120 kg/m² of vertical projection. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII (Group A dwellings), Wind Load.

q: As per NSCP, what is the minimum design live load for concrete slabs for Office Spaces?
n: Office floors carry a uniform live load of 2.4 kPa. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 205-1.

q: Which type of environmental force must be considered in the structural design of tall buildings, billboard, and roof structures due to lateral! pressure?
n: Wind load is the lateral environmental pressure that governs tall buildings, billboards and roof structures. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 207 (Wind Loads).

q: In CHB wall construction, what is the primary structural function of vertical reinforcing bars aside from ensuring load resistance, crack control and long-term durability under applied forces?
o: To counteract lateral deformation forces, serving primarily as a flexural resistance system against wind and seismic loads, with minimal axial load contribution
To enhance vertical load-bearing capacity by transferring axial forces through the wall system, preventing excessive deformation and ensuring uniform load distribution
To act as a shear-resisting component, controlling inter-block displacement and minimizing differential movement within masonry assemblies
To enhance bending rigidity by increasing moment capacity and preventing rotational instability in CHB structures
n: Vertical bars in reinforced CHB walls mainly resist flexure from out-of-plane wind and seismic forces. The masonry itself carries most of the axial load. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 7 (Masonry), reinforced masonry design; DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 1046.

q: In reinforced CHB wall construction, horizontal reinforcement bars are installed at regular intervals even when vertical reinforcement and stiffener columns are already provided. What is the MOST important structural purpose of these horizontal bars?
o: To replace the need for bond beams by providing equivalent flexural capacity throughout the wall height.
To increase the axial load-carrying capacity of the wall by transmitting gravity loads directly to the footing.
To reduce the dead load of the wall by improving force distribution between individual CHB units.
To control cracking and improve resistance to tensile and lateral forces induced by shrinkage, wind, and seismic actions.
n: Horizontal bars (joint reinforcement) control cracking from shrinkage and temperature, and add resistance to tensile and lateral (wind and seismic) forces. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Sec. 7 (Masonry); ACI 530 / TMS 402 (joint reinforcement).

q: What is the standard design live load for hotel guest rooms?
n: Hotel guest rooms (residential) carry a uniform live load of 1.9 kPa, about 200 kg/m². Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 205-1.

q: According to NSCP 2015 and standard reinforced concrete detailing practices, what is the minimum concrete cover required for cast-in-place concrete columns exposed to earth or weather, to protect reinforcement against corrosion and ensure durability?
n: Cast-in-place concrete exposed to earth or weather needs 50 mm of cover for 20 mm and larger bars (40 mm for 16 mm and smaller). Concrete cast against earth needs 75 mm. Source: NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Vol. 1, Table 420.6.1.3.1.
